To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have identified a novel microfluidics device that allows isolation of axons, and have identified >300 transcripts present in uninjury and regenerating cortical axon mRNA.
cortical axons contain a large repertoire of mRNAs and that the mRNA pool changes in response to axonal injury.

(1) we have for the 1st time identified and characterized the axonal mRNA in matured and regenerating CNS axon, (2) we have identified the presence of axonal mRNA in the CNS, and have shown that many of the axonal mRNA transcripts are similar to those found in PNS injury conditioned DRG axons, (3) we have shown that axons contain many different types of mRNAs, and that the axonal mRNA population changes after injury,
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying neuronal regeneration.
the identification, localization and characterization of axonal mRNAs and their role in axonal transport and regeneration.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the development of the nervous system, and the repair of the nervous system in disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study has shown that axons are more than passive conduits for the transport of proteins, and that the mRNA pool in axons can be modified after axonal injury.
the mRNA pool in CNS axons changes after injury.
the CNS and PNS axon transcriptome is similar, with some differences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have identified the axonal mRNA present in uninjured and regenerating CNS axon, and that the transcripts are enriched for proteins that maintain axonal transport, the cytoskeleton and mitochondria, suggesting that these are important for axonal maintenance and function.
the axon is not just a passive structure, but a highly active one, with the potential to respond rapidly to changes in its environment.
axonal mRNA is not just a remnant of the cell body, but is an important component of the axon that can respond to injury.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have identified a large number of axonal transcripts, and have shown that many of these transcripts change in their axonal localization after injury.
the axon has the ability to maintain a local protein synthesis capacity that can be altered in response to injury, which may have important implications for axonal regeneration and plasticity.
we show that axonal mRNA can be isolated from mammalian CNS axons.
